text: Okay. So I'm just gonna go through a little bit of background, which most of you are pretty familiar with, and then get right into the CDC recommendations and what this ordinance actually says. The city, in addition to the national effort, the city enacted its own efforts to flatten the curve in Norman. So proclamations were issued three in March, one in April, that kind of got progressively more restrictive as the numbers went up, ultimately limiting gathering size and limiting activities to essential activities only. Then on April 27th, our numbers were looking really good. We thought we'd flattened the curve successfully and we began a phase three opening that culminated in a return to normal activities on June 12th. So just to give you some of the data, as of April 30th, there were 213 total positive cases in Norman with 18 deaths. Between May 1st and June 15th, we were doing really well. We were averaging about one new case per day. We had two additional deaths during that six week period. In the last 22 days, we have seen an additional 327 cases of COVID-19. So the primary source of spread, and I've put the CDC sources at the top of each slide so you'll have those if you need them, it's person to person spread. So people within six feet of one another. They believe that this spreads through respiratory droplets that are produced when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or talks. It can be spread by people who are not showing symptoms. And that seems to be occurring particularly in those younger age groups, the 18 to 35 year olds. So this is part of the concern that got us to this point. The CDC is recommending to prevent COVID that you maintain good social distance, six feet between you and others outside of your household. You wash your hands often, or if you can't wash your hands with soap, use hand sanitizer. Hard to find these days, I know. That you routinely clean and disinfect frequently touched surfaces. And then you cover your mouth and nose with a cloth face covering when around others. This is directly from the CDC website about face coverings. And it talks about why it's important to wear one. And it says there that it helps prevent people who have COVID from spreading the virus to others. Wearing a face covering will help protect people around you, including those at a higher risk and people who frequently come into close contact with other people. These are people in businesses that never closed and at restaurants and stores and at the grocery store. Cloth face coverings are most likely to reduce the spread of COVID-19 when they're widely used by people in public settings. The spread can be reduced with cloth face coverings and other preventative measures like social distancing, frequent hand washing, and the cleaning and disinfecting that I talked about a minute ago. The CDC also has this guidance about why social distancing. This is a term that I thought just came along with COVID, but it's been around a lot longer than that in regards to pandemics. But it says COVID-19 spreads mainly among people who are in close contact, so within six feet for a prolonged period. The spread happens when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or talks. Droplets from their mouth or nose are launched into the air and land in the mouths or noses of people nearby. Kind of gross to think about. They can also be inhaled into the lungs and recent studies indicate, as I said, that people who are infected but do not have symptoms likely play a pretty significant role in the spread of COVID-19. Since you can spread the virus before you even know you're sick, it's important to stay at least six feet away from others when possible, even if you or they don't have any symptoms. It's especially important for people who are at higher risk for severe illness. So in this ordinance, council talked about this last week. We heard from Dr. Raskob, we heard from Richie Split at the hospital, and talked about the numbers we were seeing in Norman. And so council asked that we draft an ordinance that dealt with masks in public and also the issue of bars and public gatherings in those type of businesses. We're obviously all thinking about when the college students come back in August and how to keep the virus from spreading more rapidly and more frequently than it is now. So as a general rule in this ordinance, if you're interacting with others outside of your household, you should wear a face covering. It defines these places, places of public accommodation, public service areas, and public settings. Places of public accommodation are places offering items, goods, or services for purchase or rent. So these are like retail businesses, spas, salons, entertainment venues, food service facilities, restaurants, bars, hotels, motels, professional offices and services, banks, repair facilities, motor vehicle dealerships, anywhere where you're allowing the public in and the public is coming in to get some good or service. A public service area is a place of public accommodation where the employees interact with the public in the normal course of business. And then a public setting is any public place where persons congregate, which is not a place of public accommodation, including offices, workplaces, houses of worship, childcare facilities, hospitals, health facilities, gymnasiums, adult and youth sports facilities, communal outdoor spaces, food trucks, other outdoor retail entities. So in all of these places, the general expectation under the ordinance is that you would be wearing a face covering if you're interacting with others in those places. There are exceptions, and most of these come from practical considerations, but also from the CDC. They recognize that certain persons may not be able to wear a face covering. It could exacerbate a physical or mental health condition. It could lead to a medical emergency or introduce significant safety concerns. So those are situations where you're interacting with someone who is deaf and relies on lip reading, they need to be able to see your face. If you're someone with a developmental disability, sensory integration concerns, some cognitive ability limitations or other medical conditions that warrant accommodation. If you're engaged in an activity where the face covering is likely to become wet, that's not safe. That would be like when you're swimming. And individuals engaged in high intensity activities like running, youth sports, I've been asked about that. If wearing the mask causes difficulty breathing, they don't have to be worn. And then finally, if you work in a setting where the face covering may increase the risk of either a heat related illness or cause safety concerns due to introduction of a hazard, you're exempted from the face covering requirement. The ordinance says if you meet one of the exemptions you should consider using a face shield, but the face shield needs to wrap around the sides of your face and extend to below the chin. That's directly from the CDC as well. Persons exercising in communal outdoor spaces provided you continue to socially distance from other people outside of your household. Settings where a mask isn't feasible, you're getting your teeth cleaned or some other medical treatment, it may not be feasible to wear a mask. Of course, inside your private car and your private home or in your hotel room or inside your individual office space you would not have to wear a mask. Places of public accommodation are required to post signage at the entrances to their facility that notifies the public that a mask is required. We're working on a uniform sign for all places of public accommodation. So everyone will have the same signage and we'll be getting those out to the chamber and to other businesses as soon as that's finalized. The ordinance says that these facilities, places of public accommodation will make masks available to people seeking to enter their establishments at no charge provided. The city makes them available to the businesses for distribution. We've had some contact with a willing donor and we're working through that to see if we can't get an order of masks in pretty quickly and be able to distribute those to businesses. When someone comes to the business and doesn't have a mask, you'll have a free mask to provide them. And then social distancing, particularly as it regards restaurants and bars, and bar areas within restaurants. These are areas where you cannot wear a mask as you're eating and drinking. And so in restaurants, the ordinance says you have to arrange your seating to promote social distancing between groups of patrons. Many of our restaurants are already doing that. And then bars and bar areas within restaurants limit the capacity to the number of seats available. So no standing room only areas and arrange the seats to promote social distancing between groups of patrons. And we have in here also thinking of primarily of the larger college crowds here, a closure requirement for bars and bar areas at 10 p.m. on weekdays and 11 p.m. on weekends. Most of the questions I've gotten are about how are we going to enforce this? And let me be clear, the goal is compliance. It's not to write tickets. And as we did through the proclamations, the focus will be on education. We want to create the general expectation that everyone will wear a mask when interacting with the public, but there isn't a specific penalty for not wearing a mask. If a business chooses to deny someone entry into the business because someone refuses to wear a mask and the police get called, we have existing ordinances that can address patrons' behavior and or the preference of the business. So for example, if you're denied entry because you refuse to wear a mask and you just get in your car and go home, no issue there. If you create a scene, if you're yelling and screaming and some of these things we've seen go viral across the country, that's when the police may be called and the business could sign a complaint if they so chose to do so for disturbing the peace, they could trespass someone from the business. But those are the type of offenses that would probably come and it would be based on the patron's behavior, not their failure to wear a mask. If the business doesn't post the required signs or doesn't follow the social distancing requirements pertains to restaurants and bars, then it could be subject to a ticket. These, of course, we're gonna do education first, warnings first, but once it's ultimately, if it results in a ticket, once it's ultimately adjudicated in municipal court, it could result in a fine of 50 to $500. This is pretty unusual for a city ordinance, but we have a sunset provision in this ordinance and I know it's been a cause of concern for some, but there's a few ways the ordinance could end or expire. If the mayor rescinds the COVID-19 emergency declaration, the ordinance will automatically sunset, it wouldn't take further council action. If council takes action to repeal the ordinance, then the ordinance would automatically sunset, but if they do nothing, if nothing else changes, the ordinance automatically expires on November 30th.
